en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Similes,
Section on the Donkey.
5. The Question on the Leopard’s Limbs “Venerable Nāgasena, when you say that ‘two limbs of the leopard should be adopted,’ which are those two limbs that should be adopted?
“Just as, Great King, the leopard, having hidden himself by relying upon a thicket of grass, a thicket of forest, or a mountain cleft in the wilderness, seizes deer;”
In the same way, Great King, a yogi practicing yoga should resort to solitude: the forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen,
a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space,
or a heap of straw— a place that is quiet, free from noise, devoid of crowds, hidden from people, and suitable for seclusion.
"For, Great King, a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, by cultivating seclusion, before long attains mastery over the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*).
This, Great King, is the first quality of the lamp that should be adopted.
And this, Great King, was said by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma:"
"Just as one called a leopard,
having hidden himself, seizes a deer;
even so does this son of the Buddha."
“Practicing yoga with application and possessing insight,
having entered the forest,
he grasps the supreme fruit.”
Furthermore, great king, a leopard does not eat any animal it has killed that has fallen on its left side;
even so, great king, a practitioner, a follower of yoga, whether by giving bamboo, or giving leaves, or giving flowers, or giving fruits,
or giving bath-powder, or giving clay, or giving scented powder, or giving tooth-sticks—
or by the offering of mouthfuls of water, or out of a desire for flattery, or out of a desire for bean-soup, or out of servitude,
or by being sent on errands on foot, or by medical practice, or by acting as a messenger, or by going back and forth, or by giving alms-food in exchange for alms-food,

or by the giving of a gift in return for a gift, or by the science of site-selection, or by the science of astrology, or by the science of bodily marks, or by any other such thing censured by the Buddha.
Food produced by wrong livelihood must not be eaten, just as a leopard does not eat an animal that has fallen on its left side.
This, O Great King, is the second quality of the leopard to be adopted.
And this, O Great King, was said by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:
“If I were to eat this sweet milk-rice that has arisen through the influence of vocal intimation,
[I would surely attain enlightenment].”
That livelihood is censured by me,
even if it were to pass through my intestines and exit outside.
“Even while giving up my life, I would not break my livelihood.
Thus ends the fifth question, the Dīpikaṅga Question.
